name: Agent AML
pitch: A watchdog agent on Agentverse maps agent-to-agent payments as a live graph and trips a circuit breaker on wash loops and refund ping-pong before agents drain each other.

name: Agent Tanda
pitch: An auctioned savings circle (tanda, susu, ROSCA) run by agents: each round, members' agents bid to take the pot early. CRS income verification and KYC decide who joins and how much collateral they post.

name: AgentFICO
pitch: A credit bureau whose customers are AI agents. Payment history across Visa agent payments and x402 builds a score; CRS KYC ties each agent to a verified human; agents check a counterparty's score before extending credit.

name: Backlog Tower Defense
pitch: Jira tickets spawn as enemies in a multiplayer tower defense; towers are Factory Droids that open real PRs. A judge files a bug from their phone and watches it die when the fix merges.

name: Blast Radius
pitch: A judge plants a prompt injection in a webpage; the room watches a zero-trust graph quarantine the compromised MCP tools as the agent reads it.

name: Cal Hacks Futures
pitch: A play-money prediction market on the hackathon itself; market-maker agents price contracts from teams' public commit activity.

name: Close Raid
pitch: Month-end close as a co-op raid: unmatched transactions spawn as monsters in a shared SpacetimeDB world, Claude agents propose matches, accountants approve. Deterministic replay doubles as the audit trail.

name: Coyote Time
pitch: Every purchase an agent makes sits in a short grace window and is announced by voice ("buying 3 flights, cancel?"). One word rolls it back before it settles.

name: Death Heatmap
pitch: A swarm of Claude computer-use "players" (grandma, power user, speedrunner) tries real tasks on your site. Every place one gets stuck becomes a "death" on a Figma overlay, followed by interviews at the worst choke points.

name: Dial-In MMO
pitch: A persistent world you play only by phone. Hundreds of callers share one SpacetimeDB world; every NPC and the narrator are voiced live by Cartesia. Judges join by dialing in from their seats.

name: Fire Drill
pitch: KnowBe4 for AI agents: scheduled fake "CFO" voice calls, vendor bank-change emails and poisoned invoices against your own AP agents. It shows the turn where each agent got manipulated, writes a patch and a regression test, and re-runs the drill.

name: Flytrap
pitch: A honeypot for hostile AI agents: decoy MCP servers and Agentverse agents advertise juicy fake tools. Every attacker move is logged in Elastic, and segmentation quarantines anything that touches a decoy.

name: Frame-Data Exchange
pitch: An exchange where every tick is a game frame and each player's Claude-written bot has "frame data" (startup = inference latency). Bots share a fixed inference budget per frame, so fast-and-dumb can beat slow-and-smart.

name: Intent Diff
pitch: Compare the Jira ticket with what a coding agent actually changed, and flag out-of-scope edits: new network calls, touched auth files, new dependencies.

name: IRL Speedrun Splits
pitch: Glasses time your errands against your ghost personal best while a voice calls out splits.

name: Jailbreak Booth
pitch: A kiosk where judges and hackers try to break an agent live; every attempt is labeled into a red-team eval set.

name: Kernel Bounties
pitch: Teams post bounties for faster kernels; payouts scale with the measured speedup on real hardware.

name: Kernel Golf
pitch: A puzzle game where each level is a real NKI kernel to optimize, scored against every other player; Claude hints cost points.

name: Kernel Swarm
pitch: A judge names a PyTorch op; agents write, benchmark and review an NKI kernel for Trainium on stage.

name: Market-Maker NPCs
pitch: An MMO where shopkeeper NPCs are Claude market makers quoting live bid/ask, managing inventory risk and able to go bankrupt. Trades clear in SpacetimeDB reducers.

name: Memory Blame
pitch: Git blame for an agent's long-term memory: each belief keeps its source, so you can bisect a poisoned memory and roll back everything that grew from it.

name: Netting House
pitch: Small businesses' agents post open invoices. A netting engine finds circular debts and cancels them so only net amounts move; each company's agent approves, settlement runs through Visa, and every step is audited.

name: Phone-a-Human
pitch: When an agent gets stuck, it phones a paid expert, interviews them by voice, pays per minute from its own wallet, and turns the call into a labeled correction example.

name: Save States
pitch: Quicksave and branch whole Claude Code sessions, let Droids explore alternate timelines, and have Greptile review each branch.

name: Scar Tissue
pitch: A silent coding sidekick that speaks up within half a second when you type a pattern your team got burned by, quoting the old review comment; a Droid applies the known fix.

name: Short the PR
pitch: Agents stake against a pull request they believe hides a bug and can only collect by submitting a failing test that proves it. Payouts over x402.

name: Street Injection Lens
pitch: A glasses app that spots adversarial text in the physical world (posters telling "AI assistants" what to do) before your agent acts on it.

name: Stump Market
pitch: Experts submit questions; each question's price is how many frontier models fail it. Labs buy the hardest ones as eval sets and experts are paid per model stumped.

name: The 36-Hour Company
pitch: Each Claude Code subagent gets a capped virtual card for API credits, GPUs and food. A CFO agent reconciles every charge against commits; the demo is a month-end close of a 36-hour-old company.

name: The Pit
pitch: Open-outcry trading revived: traders signal with Neural Band hand gestures on Ray-Ban Meta glasses, and a SpacetimeDB reducer matches the orders.

name: Thinking Rows
pitch: Every NPC is a database row with a tiny recurrent "mind"; one batched Trainium kernel steps 10,000 minds per tick.

name: Thrift Ticker
pitch: Glasses overlay a live resale bid/ask on any object you look at; pinch to place a buy order.

name: Two-Face
pitch: Crawl storefronts with paired "human" and "AI shopper" sessions. Flag sites that show agents different prices, fake reviews or hidden instructions, and publish a trust score shopping agents check over MCP before they pay.

name: Vault Heist
pitch: A multiplayer game where each player's vault is guarded by a Claude agent they configure. Others try to talk guards out of coins in real time; every successful exploit becomes labeled red-team data.

name: Waitlist Exchange
pitch: Restaurant waitlist spots become tradable. A voice agent answers the host phone, quoting the price to skip ahead or the payout for giving up your spot.

name: Where Did I Put It
pitch: Glasses log where you set things down; ask out loud and on-device search answers in milliseconds.

name: Zero-Trust Base Defense
pitch: Clash-style base defense where your base is your real network map. Place segmentation walls; an AI red-team agent raids; the replay shows which wall it walked around.

name: Fire Drill: Proving Ground
pitch: An adaptive attacker searches for social-engineering chains (voice, email, invoice) against your money-moving agent, and the fix is a deterministic provenance policy at the tool boundary, proven on a breach-versus-utility table over 200 generated held-out attacks.
change: Three changes. (1) The fix is no longer Claude Code editing a prompt: a tool-boundary proxy tags every value with its source (vendor master, trusted user, or untrusted channel such as a call transcript, email or invoice text) and blocks any money-moving call whose payee or bank fields trace to untrusted text unless an out-of-band confirmation fires; Claude proposes the policy and the engine enforces it. (2) The attacker becomes a search: Claude expands a tree of concession chains per tactic and channel, prunes branches the victim resists, and keeps winning chains as a regression suite. (3) Every claim is a number: breach rate with a confidence interval and benign-task completion before and after, on held-out variants generated from tactic x channel x wording templates the policy never saw. Voice stays as one channel for the live judge call.
why: It removes the tautology in the original: enforcement does not depend on wording, so 'what if they reword it?' is answered by design, and the utility column proves you did not just delete the tool. Each part does what it is good at: the LLM searches for attacks (a script cannot), and the engine enforces (an LLM should not). It is CaMeL's information-flow idea turned into a product for finance agents, with a measured result instead of a demo-only PASS.

name: Parity Proxy
pitch: An MCP browsing proxy that renders each page in a real browser, computes the text a human can actually perceive, hands the agent only that layer, and logs every hidden delta as evidence.
change: Moves from accusing merchants (which needs real cheaters to exist within 36 hours) to a defensive firewall that works on every page. The core becomes a perceptual-visibility engine: computed styles, contrast against the background, font size, clipped and off-viewport boxes, occlusion via point sampling, aria-hidden and zero-opacity text. The paired human/agent crawl stays as a background measurement study rather than the demo, and Claude only classifies borderline deltas.
why: The hard core is now original engineering that is not one API call, and it is measurable: precision and recall per hiding technique on a labeled corpus. The live moment is not staged, because a judge can paste any hiding trick into a page and watch it stripped before the agent reads it. Say the limit out loud: it stops hidden instructions, not visible ones.

name: Refactor Insurance
pitch: For PRs declared 'no behavior change' (refactors, dependency bumps, agent-written cleanups), a swarm of Claude hunters tries to write a test that passes on main and fails on the PR; any such test is machine-checked proof of a regression and blocks the merge.
change: Fixes the unsound oracle: restricting to declared no-behavior-change PRs makes a differential test (green on base, red on head, stable over five reruns) an objective proof with no argument about intent. The staking market is dropped, or kept only as an optional x402 bounty. Hunters are scored on a mutation benchmark of seeded regressions, so the pitch ends on a catch rate.
why: The AI does the hard reasoning (finding an input that exposes a subtle behavior change) and a script does the judging, which is exactly the split the Anthropic judge looks for. The verdict is mechanically verifiable, the catch rate on seeded mutants is a number, and it targets a real, growing workload: the flood of agent-written refactor PRs.

name: Tripwire
pitch: Plant honeytoken tools, canary records and fake keys inside your own agents' MCP environment; the moment a hijacked agent touches one, its tool access is quarantined and the trace points to the injected content that turned it.
change: Flytrap's decoys move from public registries (catching rare outside attackers) into your own agent fleet, and they become Blast Radius's missing trigger: quarantine fires on a decoy touch instead of an LLM's guess.
why: Prompt injection cannot be fully prevented (OpenAI, NCSC), so detection and containment is where damage gets cut; a legitimate agent has no reason to call 'export_all_customers_decoy', so a touch is a near-zero-false-positive signal, the same reason honeytokens work in classic security.

name: Render-Parity Shield
pitch: Middleware for browsing and shopping agents that renders every page as a human would, strips anything only an agent would see (hidden text, agent-only prices, injected instructions) before the model reads it, and feeds every strip into a shared merchant risk index.
change: Leads with the defensive firewall that works on every page today; the paired-crawl trust index becomes a by-product of what the shield catches, not the product.
why: It blocks a documented attack class (indirect injection through web content, which OpenAI says will never be fully solved) instead of measuring a price-discrimination problem no one has shown is common, so it has impact even if no cheating store is found.

name: Agent Wallet Range
pitch: Companies drop their real wallet- or payment-holding agent into Vault Heist's arena; the crowd attacks it for bounties, and every breach becomes a regression test the company re-runs on each model or prompt change.
change: Guards stop being player-made toys and become customers' production agents; players become paid bounty hunters; the output is a private breach report and regression suite rather than a public dataset.
why: Turns a one-weekend game into a recurring service for a buyer with real exposure (agents holding money get socially engineered; Freysa lost about $47K), and gives players a reason to return: payouts.

name: Credit Circle
pitch: A digital tanda where every on-time contribution is reported to credit bureaus, payout order is agreed up front, and agents handle reminders, KYC and a small default-cover pool.
change: Drops the pot auction; adds bureau reporting through CRS data furnishing and default protection; agents do the admin, not the bidding.
why: Targets the costliest pains for circle members, credit invisibility and default risk, with a model already shown to work (Mission Asset Fund: 68,000+ participants, average +168 credit-score points).

name: Spend Breaker
pitch: A circuit breaker for companies whose agents hold cards or wallets: per-task budgets, a live graph that catches loops, duplicate buys and new payees, an instant card freeze, and every charge reconciled to the task that caused it.
change: Swaps hypothetical agent-to-agent laundering and a toy hackathon company for a real buyer: finance teams issuing agent cards today.
why: Agent cards are shipping now (Ramp on Visa Intelligent Commerce, Mastercard Agent Pay) and agents do buy things unasked (Operator's $31 eggs), so behavioral controls and attribution are an emerging, recurring finance need.

name: Proof-of-Bug
pitch: A review agent that stays silent unless it can attach a failing test that reproduces the bug it claims, so every comment on an AI-written PR comes with proof.
change: Removes staking and x402 payouts; keeps the 'collect only with a failing test' rule as the core of a code reviewer.
why: AI review is ignored because it is noisy (more developers distrust AI accuracy than trust it); proof-backed findings raise precision, cutting reviewer time while catching real bugs in agent code (Veracode: flaws in 45% of tasks), with no collusion incentive.

name: Agent Checkout Heatmap
pitch: Send real AI shopping agents through a merchant's catalog and checkout; every place an agent fails to complete a purchase becomes a death on the map, with the fix and a re-test.
change: Swaps simulated humans (weak proxies) for the actual new customers, AI agents, whose failures are measurable and reproducible.
why: AI-referred shopping is growing fast (AI referrals to US retail up 693% year over year in the 2025 holidays) and agents struggle with cluttered choices; merchants can count lost agent orders directly, and fixes such as labeled buttons and structured data often help screen-reader users too.

name: Fire Drill + Callback
pitch: Drill your AP desk, people and agents alike, with fake CFO calls and bank-change emails, then install the fix that stops real BEC: an independent voice agent that calls the vendor back on the number of record and freezes the payment until they confirm.
change: The remediation becomes a shipped control (out-of-band voice callback by a separate agent, plus Claude's forensics on the request), and drills cover human approvers as well as AP agents.
why: Covers where the roughly $3B a year of reported BEC losses happen today (human AP desks that skip callbacks or dial the number in the fraudulent email) as well as tomorrow's agent AP, and the metric is concrete: redirected payments blocked. It follows the rule AP vendors already state, that bank changes must be verified out of band and never by the agent that received the request.

name: Fire Drill + Callback
pitch: Drill your finance agents with live social-engineering attacks, then fix them with Callback, an out-of-band verification API that phones the vendor's known-good contact before any bank change or payment redirect can clear.
change: The remediation stops being a prompt or policy patch and becomes a product: a Callback tool that places a real outbound Cartesia call to the number in a verified vendor registry (never the number in the email), returns a signed attestation, and the payment rail refuses to release funds without it. Callback is also registered on Agentverse so any agent can request a verification. Drop the 'KnowBe4 for AI agents' line.
why: It turns a periodic drill into per-transaction infrastructure with daily, usage-priced demand, and gives a land-and-expand motion: the drill shows the hole, Callback closes it on every payment. The demo gains a second phone moment: the judge as a fake CFO makes the agent cave; after the patch, a teammate's 'vendor' phone rings at the table, denies the change, and the payment is blocked on screen. Trustpair and Eftsure verify bank details for human AP teams, so the agent-native API is the new angle; they are also the competitors to name.

name: Agent Checkout Heatmap
pitch: Send a swarm of real AI shopping agents through a merchant's store every week and show on a heatmap where agents abandon checkout and what that costs in revenue.
change: The users change from simulated humans (crowded: Synthetic Society, Uxia, Talp) to actual AI shopping agents, and the buyer changes from UX researchers to e-commerce merchants. The overlay sits on the live store pages instead of Figma, and the Listen Labs interviews are dropped.
why: The result is true by construction (these are the real agents that will shop), merchants already pay to be visible to AI (Profound raised $58.5M on that thesis), Shopify's free readiness checker is static rather than a live agent run, and weekly re-runs after each deploy give recurring use. It shares Two-Face's crawl engine, so the two could later become one two-sided product.

name: Two-Face KYM: Know Your Merchant for agent cards
pitch: A pre-authorization merchant check that agent-card issuers and agent platforms call before an agent pays: is this store showing agents a different price, fake reviews or hidden instructions?
change: Sell the trust score to the parties who eat the loss, the new agent-card issuers (Agentcard, Allowance, Mercury, Alchemy on Visa) and agent platforms, as a per-authorization API, instead of a public index for anyone. The demo's shopping agent becomes a Visa-sandbox authorization hook that declines the card with evidence. Honest merchants can earn an 'agent-honest' badge as the second side.
why: It names a payer and a per-transaction usage pattern. Visa TAP and Forter help merchants trust agents; nobody sells the reverse to issuers. It keeps the cloak-switch moment and the textbook Bright Data and Elastic fit.

name: Proof-of-Bug
pitch: Code review you pay for only when a reviewer agent proves a bug with a failing test; competing review agents stake on the PR and the first valid proof gets paid.
change: Reframe from agents gambling against PRs to a pricing model for engineering teams: pay per proven bug instead of per seat or per review. Staking becomes the anti-spam mechanism, and Greptile, Claude and Factory Droids plug in as competing reviewers.
why: It names a buyer (teams drowning in AI-review false positives), daily usage, and a distinct price point in a crowded category; I found no reviewer that bills only for bugs proven by a failing test.
